questions.q: What does the CAP theorem actually say?
options: Consistency and availability can never both exist in any system, partitioned or not
A distributed system can always provide consistency, availability, and partition tolerance simultaneously
Partition tolerance is an optional feature that most systems don't need
When a network partition occurs, a system must choose between consistency and availability
questions.explain: CAP specifically describes behavior during an actual partition: the system must sacrifice either consistency or availability — it cannot fully guarantee both at that moment.

questions.q: Why is "pick any 2 of 3" considered a misleading summary of CAP?
options: Because partition tolerance isn't optional in a real multi-machine system — partitions happen eventually regardless of choice
Because availability is impossible in any distributed system
Because CAP doesn't apply to any real-world system
Because consistency and availability are actually the same thing
questions.explain: Network partitions are a fact of operating multiple machines over a network; you can't opt out of partition tolerance the way you can choose between C and A.

questions.q: What does PACELC add that CAP alone does not cover?
options: A fourth letter standing for "Performance"
The latency-versus-consistency trade-off that exists even when there is no partition
A requirement that all systems must be strongly consistent
A proof that CAP is incorrect
questions.explain: PACELC extends CAP by noting that even during normal operation (no partition), systems still trade latency against consistency because coordination between replicas takes time.

questions.q: A strongly consistent configuration store refuses to answer a read it can't confirm is current. What CAP behavior is this?
options: Ignoring the CAP theorem entirely
A violation of partition tolerance
Favoring consistency over availability (a CP choice)
Favoring availability over consistency (an AP choice)
questions.explain: Refusing to serve a possibly-stale read during a partition, rather than risk incorrect data, is the classic CP (consistency-favoring) choice.

questions.q: Why might a DNS resolver or shopping cart service choose to keep answering with possibly stale data during a partition?
options: Because stale data is always more accurate than fresh data
Because CAP does not apply to read-heavy systems
Because DNS and shopping carts are not distributed systems
Because an available-but-possibly-stale answer is more useful to the user than an error page, which is an AP (availability-favoring) choice
questions.explain: Systems like DNS and shopping carts typically favor availability: continuing to serve an answer, even a possibly stale one, is more valuable to users than refusing to respond.
